extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and advanced law students (practitioners in patent claim drafting and litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal principles for interpreting (construing) patent specifications, drawings, and claims, including how phrases, references, prior art, and prosecution history affect claim scope and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the patent's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing described in letters patent, is secured thereby, unless it is covered by a claim, and no element not mentioned in a claim can be read into it even though the element appears in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent secures only what its claims cover. Do not import unclaimed elements from the specification into the claim. Example/anti-pattern: attempting to assert protection for a feature present only in the description but not in any claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims control construction of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of letters patent depends therefore upon the construction of their respective claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation work should begin with the claims; the established rules for construing claims govern the meaning and scope of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a claim narrower or broader than the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which is clearly narrower than the invention which it was designed to cover, cannot be broadened by construction... Nor can a claim, which is broader than the state of the art will allow to the invention described, be narrowed by a construction out of harmony with its language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must respect the literal language of the claim: they cannot judicially broaden an unduly narrow claim, nor artificially narrow a broadly worded claim contrary to its language. Balance must be kept with prior art and validity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and import of 'substantially as described' / 'as specified'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'substantially as described,' or its equivalent, when such a phrase occurs in a claim, throws the investigator back to the description for means of construction; and that phrase is always implied in claims wherein it is not expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrases (expressed or implied) direct construction toward the specification and drawings with respect to the particular matter claimed, but they will not import into a claim any unessential feature or unnecessary detail. Some courts have given special narrowing effect to the phrase; Supreme Court decisions caution not to add elements not already in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncommon claim terms construed in light of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: An uncommon word in a claim is to be construed in the light of the description, rather than in the light of the dictionary;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patentee used an unusual term, presume the reader will consult the specification; interpret such terms according to the patentee's description, not solely by dictionary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imply 'for the purpose set forth' in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'for the purpose set forth' is never implied in a claim, because an inventor is entitled to the exclusive use of his invention for all purposes, whether he sets them all forth in his specification or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting or interpreting claims as limited to stated purposes; including such a phrase is discouraged because it cannot validate an otherwise void claim and may enable design-arounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of limiting words like 'in mechanism'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'in mechanism' is used in many claims, with a purpose to limit the claim ... to the subject of that claim where that subject is employed as a part of a particular mechanism. Such a limitation is effective to exclude later employment ... in other mechanism, and thus to negative infringement; but such a limitation is not effective to exclude earlier employment ... and thus to avert negation of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting a claim to use 'in mechanism' narrows infringement scope (environment-dependent) but does not change novelty determinations; novelty depends on the character of the invention, not environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of drawings in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings attached to letters patent may be referred to for explanation of anything which the description leaves obscure, but not to supply a total omission of description, or to contradict any plain statement therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drawings to clarify obscurities only. Do not use drawings to fill in a complete missing description or to contradict explicit specification text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neither drawings nor descriptions can enlarge claims
rubrics_metrics.description: And neither drawings nor descriptions can enlarge claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification/drawings cannot be used to broaden the express scope of the claims. They may, however, justify narrowing a claim by showing necessary elements for operativeness/novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: When description may narrow a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be narrowed by limitations in the description, and also by importation by construction of described elements which are necessary to invention or novelty as well as operativeness; or are necessary to operativeness alone; but not such as are necessary only to invention or novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may construe a claim narrowly by importing elements from the description if those elements are necessary for the invention to operate or to distinguish over the prior art; but do not import elements that are only incidentally described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference letters/numerals do not automatically limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference letters or numerals, when used in a claim to indicate, or to help indicate, a part or combination covered thereby, do not limit that claim to the specific mechanism shown in the patent; unless the claim must be thus limited by the prior state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using reference numerals in claims is generally illustrative, not limiting. However, if novelty resides exclusively in the particular characteristics shown and identified, the claim will be limited to those particular characteristics to avoid lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific references imply materiality of referenced parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part specifically referred to by a letter is deemed material according to the well known doctrine...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification labels parts (e.g., vessel A, A', C, C'), those labeled characteristics are deemed material; a reader must assume those characteristics (or equivalents) are required for the part in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims limited to means that produce the result
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims which are functional in form; that is to say, claims which literally purport to cover a result rather than a process or a thing, are properly construed to cover only the process or the thing which produces that result, for otherwise such claims would be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim phrased by result must be read as covering the specific means/process/thing disclosed that achieves the result; purely result-oriented claim language will not be permitted to stand if it would otherwise be indefinite or void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that mix machine and process - constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: It has ... been held that if a process claim be combined with a claim for a machine the process must be capable of being carried out by other means than the machine of the patent and such means must be known, otherwise the process claim will be regarded as a claim for the function of the machine and hence invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting/reading both machine and process claims, ensure the process is not limited to the machine unless alternative means are known; otherwise the process claim risks invalidity as an attempt to claim the machine's function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascribing a function to an element limits the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim ascribes a function, to any of the things which it specifies, that ascription is a limitation of that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim element is defined by the function it performs, this functional language narrows the scope to elements performing that function (and may affect equivalents analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defined by process of manufacture limited to product made
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim defines its subject by reference to the character which results from making it by a particular process, that claim is limited to the article as thus produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the distinguishing feature is the process-result, the claim covers the article only as produced by that process; alternatives producing different character may fall outside the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material-based article claims limited by specific material in description
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for an article of manufacture ... which designates its distinguishing thing by naming the material of which it is made, but which uses a generic name for that purpose; will be limited by construction, to the specific material specified in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a generic material name in a claim will be construed in light of the specific material(s) disclosed—do not assume broad coverage over all materials unless the specification supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art and state of the art must inform claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior state of the art, to which an invention belongs, must be considered in construing any claim for that invention, although the art may have been advanced to that stage, by a prior invention of the same inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims against the background of the relevant prior art (patents, uses, printed publications, drawings). The state of the art narrows the territory available to the patentee and affects how claims are given meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art in other fields may be considered with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior state of other arts, may also be considered in construing a claim; because that construction may depend on the area of the territory which was open to the claimant to cover; ... But an invention which was not designed by its maker, nor actually used, nor apparently adapted to perform the function of the claimed invention, but which was used in a remote art, under radically different conditions, to perform another function, does not limit the scope of the invention as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-field prior art can be relevant to construction where it meaningfully reduces the patentee's available territory; remote art under different conditions typically should not restrict claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrines distinguishing primary and secondary patents (breadth of construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent which is the first to give to the world an invention for doing a particular part of the world's work, is a primary patent, and is entitled to have a broad construction; but a patent which is not thus primary, is limited to the identical means, and mode of operation which it describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary patents (first in the field) receive broader construction and may be enforced against equivalents; secondary/derivative patents are construed more narrowly and tied to disclosed means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents vs. improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The original inventor of a machine will have a right to treat as infringers all who make machines operating on the same principle, and performing the same functions, by analogous means, or equivalent combinations; even though the infringing machine be an improvement on the original, and patentable as such. But if the invention claimed be itself but an improvement on a known machine ... the patentee cannot treat another as an infringer who has improved the original machine by use of a different form or combination performing the same functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the doctrine of equivalents more strongly to primary inventions; an improver's patent cannot use equivalents to suppress other non-colorable improvements. Consider which inventive step is 'primary' when assessing equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents entitled to liberal construction to preserve inventor's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for inventions are to receive a liberal construction ... are, if practicable, to be so interpreted as to uphold and not to destroy the right of the inventor. ... In a case of doubt, where the claim is fairly susceptible of two constructions, that one will be adopted, which will preserve to the patentee his actual invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim admits two reasonable constructions, prefer the one that preserves the inventor's actual invention, so long as it is consistent with the claim language. Liberality should not interpolate or add matter not present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction may be narrow to preserve validity
rubrics_metrics.description: That liberality as often shows itself in a narrow construction as in a broad one; for narrow construction may be as necessary to establish the validity of a patent, as a broad construction is to lay the foundation for proof of its infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe claims narrowly where needed to avoid anticipation or invalidity from the prior art; interpretive choice depends on preserving validity or enabling infringement proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success and public use affect construction
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been held ... that when no practical use has been made of the patent the claims will be narrowly construed, the reason for so holding being that in such a case the patent lacks the support that comes from public acquiescence. And ... where the invention is a practical success and constitutes a distinct advance in the art the claims are entitled to a liberal construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider commercial success/practical adoption as a factor: practical success supports broader (liberal) construction; absence of public use supports narrower construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history and PTO actions can preserve breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor will claims be narrowed where the proceedings in the Patent Office clearly show that the inventor intended to claim and the Patent Office intended to grant the broader monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prosecution record demonstrates both applicant and PTO intended broader coverage, courts should not construe the claim narrowly in contradiction of that record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode/expressed alternatives may affect construction
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is true that by statutory provision an inventor ... 'shall explain ... the best mode' ... it is not clear how this requirement has any bearing on the scope of his claims. The court has apparently given a broader construction to a patent in which the inventor has stated as a conclusion that there might be alternatives for the device described and shown by him, than it would have done had that statement been absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit statement in the specification that alternatives exist may support a broader claim construction; absence of such disclaimers may weigh against reading alternatives into the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents take rank by patent number or application date
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of a particular art ... includes whatever inventions ... had been already invented and used in the United States, or patented, or described in any printed publication, in any country. And an invention is patented in the eye of this law, where it is fully shown in the drawings of a patent, though not described in the specification. Patents take rank in an art in the order of their numbers; except where that order is different from the order of the dates upon which they were applied for, in which case they take rank in the order of those dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing prior art and relative priority among patents, consider patent numbers and application dates to determine ranking; drawings can constitute a patent disclosure for prior art purposes.
